ARTICLE IV: POWERS AND DUTIES

4.1 The Bureau shall have the power to:

(a) acquire by donation, purchase, bequest, or loan any materials relevant to its mission;
(b) enter into agreements with donors and lenders respecting the terms of acquisition and use;
(c) employ such officers and staff as may be necessary;
(d) publish catalogues, guides, and other scholarly works;
(e) provide advisory services to families and community organisations; and
(f) undertake such other activities as may be conducive to the fulfilment of its mission.

4.2 The Bureau shall maintain a register of all accessions, with such particulars as the Board may prescribe.

4.3 The Bureau shall take all reasonable measures to ensure the physical security and environmental stability of the materials in its custody.

ARTICLE V: ORGANISATION

5.1 The affairs of the Bureau shall be managed by a Board of Directors, to be appointed by the Minister.

5.2 The Board shall consist of not fewer than seven and not more than eleven members, of whom one shall be appointed Chairman.

5.3 The day-to-day administration of the Bureau shall be the responsibility of a Director, who shall be appointed by the Board and shall hold office on such terms and conditions as the Board may determine.

5.4 The Director shall be assisted by such deputy directors, archivists, conservators, and clerical staff as the Board may authorise.

5.5 The Board may establish such committees as it deems necessary, including an Acquisitions Committee, a Preservation Committee, and a Public Programmes Committee.

ARTICLE VI: FOUNDING OFFICERS

Singapore Family Heritage Bureau founded_on 1965-04-01 date. Record status: current.

6.1 The following persons were appointed as the founding officers of the Bureau, effective 1965-04-01:

(a) Mr. Lim Cheng Huat, Chairman of the Board;
(b) Dr. Tan Swee Lian, Director;
(c) Mr. Goh Keng Leong, Deputy Director (Collections);
(d) Mrs. Ratna Menon, Deputy Director (Preservation);
(e) Mr. Lee Kim Seng, Registrar;
(f) Miss Patricia Wong, Head of Public Services; and
(g) Mr. Abdul Rahman bin Osman, Head of Outreach.

6.2 The officers named in Clause 6.1 shall serve at the pleasure of the Board, and their successors shall be appointed in accordance with Article V.

ARTICLE VII: ACQUISITIONS POLICY

7.1 The Bureau shall give priority to materials that document the lives of ordinary families, including but not limited to:

(a) birth, marriage, and death certificates;
(b) family photographs and albums;
(c) letters, diaries, and memoirs;
(d) household account books and ration cards;
(e) school records and exercise books; and
(f) such other items as the Board may from time to time designate.

7.2 Materials offered to the Bureau shall be accepted only with the written consent of the donor, and the Bureau shall respect any conditions attached to such consent.

7.3 No material shall be accessioned unless its provenance is, to the best of the Bureau's knowledge, lawful and its title clear.

ARTICLE VIII: ACCESS AND CONFIDENTIALITY

8.1 The collections of the Bureau shall be open to members of the public for research, subject to such rules as the Board may prescribe.

8.2 Materials containing personal information shall be subject to restricted access for such period as the Board may determine, having regard to the sensitivity of the information and the wishes of the donor.

8.3 The Bureau shall not disclose any information obtained from donors or researchers except as required by law or with the consent of the person concerned.
ARTICLE IX: PRESERVATION AND CONSERVATION

9.1 The Bureau shall maintain a programme of preservation and conservation for all materials in its custody, having regard to the condition of the materials and the resources available to the Bureau from time to time.

9.2 The Deputy Director (Preservation) shall be responsible for the care of the collections, including:

(a) the monitoring of storage conditions, including temperature, humidity, and light levels;
(b) the inspection of materials upon accession and at such intervals as may be practicable;
(c) the repair and stabilisation of damaged materials, where feasible; and
(d) the making of surrogates, including microfilm and photographic copies, for materials of exceptional value or fragility.

9.3 Where the original of any material is at risk of deterioration, the Bureau may make a surrogate copy for research use and restrict access to the original, subject to the provisions of Article VIII.

9.4 No item in the custody of the Bureau shall be disposed of except with the approval of the Board, and any such disposal shall be recorded in the register maintained under Article X.

ARTICLE X: REGISTRATION AND CATALOGUING

10.1 The Registrar shall maintain a register of all materials accessioned by the Bureau, showing in respect of each item:

(a) the date of accession;
(b) the name and address of the donor;
(c) a description of the material;
(d) any conditions attached to its use; and
(e) the present location of the material.

10.2 The Bureau shall prepare catalogues and finding aids to the collections and shall update them from time to time as may be practicable.

10.3 The Registrar shall assign a unique accession number to each item or group of items, and such number shall be marked on the material or its container in a manner that does not damage the material.

ARTICLE XI: PUBLIC SERVICES AND OUTREACH

11.1 The Head of Public Services shall be responsible for the reading room and for assisting members of the public in their use of the collections.

11.2 The reading room shall be open on such days and at such hours as the Board may determine, and the rules for its use shall be posted therein.

11.3 The Bureau shall, through its Head of Outreach, organise programmes to encourage public interest in family history and in the preservation of family records. Such programmes may include exhibitions, talks, workshops, and publications.

11.4 The Bureau may cooperate with schools, universities, and other institutions in Singapore and abroad for the purpose of advancing genealogical research and the preservation of family heritage.

ARTICLE XII: PUBLICATIONS

12.1 The Bureau may publish such catalogues, guides, and other works as may further its objects.

12.2 All publications of the Bureau shall acknowledge the sources from which the materials reproduced therein are drawn, and shall comply with any conditions attached to the use of such materials.

ARTICLE XIII: FINANCE

13.1 The funds of the Bureau shall consist of:

(a) grants and subventions from the Government of Singapore;
(b) donations and bequests;
(c) fees for services rendered; and
(d) such other moneys as may lawfully be received by the Bureau.

13.2 The accounts of the Bureau shall be kept in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles and shall be audited annually by an auditor appointed by the Board.

13.3 No member of the Board or officer of the Bureau shall benefit personally from any transaction entered into on behalf of the Bureau, except for the reimbursement of expenses properly incurred.

Research Grants are intended to support original genealogical research that contributes to the public understanding of Singapore's social history. These grants may be used to defray the costs of travel to archives, purchase of reproductions of records, engagement of research assistants, and transcription services.

4.2 Publication Grants

Publication Grants are intended to support the production and dissemination of genealogical works, including printed family histories, digital databases, and curated exhibitions. Publication Grants may cover printing costs, editorial services, and the development of accompanying educational materials.

4.3 Community Engagement Grants

Community Engagement Grants are intended for Family Associations and Voluntary Welfare Organisations that wish to organise workshops, talks, or outreach programmes to encourage broader participation in genealogical research within their communities.

4.4 The maximum amount that may be awarded under any single Grant is subject to the limits specified in the Scheme's Funding Guidelines, which are issued separately and updated from time to time. Applicants are encouraged to consult the latest edition of the Funding Guidelines before submitting an application.

5. APPLICATION PROCEDURE (SUMMARY)

5.1 Applications must be submitted on the prescribed form, available from the Scheme's website or from the National Heritage Board's Resource Centre.

5.2 Each application must include a detailed project proposal, a budget breakdown, and a timeline for completion. Supporting documents, such as letters of endorsement from community organisations or evidence of prior research, may be attached.

5.3 Applications are assessed in the order in which they are received. The Committee aims to inform applicants of its decision within eight (8) weeks of receipt of a complete application.

5.4 Transitional Arrangements: Applicants who submitted a complete application before 01 July 2018 but have not yet received a decision will have their application assessed under the provisions of the previous Policy (Version 1.0), except where the current Policy is more favourable to the applicant.

6. REVIEW AND APPROVAL PROCESS

6.1 All applications are reviewed by at least two members of the Committee, who will assess the application against the eligibility criteria set out in the separate Eligibility Criteria Schedule (Annex A).

6.2 The Committee may, at its discretion, seek external expert opinion on the technical merits of a proposed project.

6.3 The Committee's decision is final. No correspondence will be entertained regarding the merits of individual applications.

**9. APPLICATION PROCEDURES**

9.1 Applications shall be made on the prescribed application form, which may be obtained from the National Heritage Board website or requested by post, email, or in person at the address given in Section 7.

9.2 The application form shall be completed in full and accompanied by the following supporting documents:

(a) A detailed project proposal, including the project title, objectives, methodology, expected outcomes, and a timeline for completion;

(b) A detailed budget, indicating the total project cost, the amount of grant requested, and the sources of any other funding, whether confirmed or pending;

(c) A curriculum vitae of the principal applicant and, where applicable, of any co-applicants or key personnel;

(d) Where the applicant is an organisation, a copy of its constitution or memorandum and articles of association, and its latest annual report or financial statements, if available;

(e) Letters of support from at least two referees who are able to comment on the applicant’s capability to undertake the proposed project; and

(f) Any other documents that the Committee may reasonably require to assess the application.

9.3 Incomplete applications will be returned to the applicant for resubmission. The date of receipt of a complete application shall be recorded by the Secretariat and shall be used for the purposes of Section 5.3.

9.5 Applications may be submitted at any time during the period of this Policy. There is no fixed application window, and the Committee will consider applications on a rolling basis, subject to the availability of funds.

9.6 The Committee reserves the right to close the Scheme to new applications at any time if the allocated budget for the financial year has been fully committed. Notice of such closure shall be published on the National Heritage Board website and, where practicable, communicated to applicants who have not yet submitted an application.

11. Community Ties

11.1 The Committee recognises that heritage is rooted in communities, and that projects are most likely to be effective when they are grounded in strong community ties. Accordingly, applicants are encouraged to demonstrate, in their project proposal, the nature and extent of their connections to the community or communities that are the subject of the project.

11.2 Community ties may be demonstrated in a variety of ways, including but not limited to:

(a) A record of prior involvement with the community, whether in a personal, professional, or volunteer capacity;

(b) Letters of support from community leaders, religious institutions, clan associations, or other local bodies;

(c) Evidence of past projects or activities undertaken with or for the community;

(d) A description of the applicant’s current relationship with the community, including any ongoing commitments or responsibilities; and

(e) Any other evidence that the applicant considers relevant to demonstrating community ties.

11.4 The Committee will consider the totality of the evidence provided, and will not apply a fixed formula in assessing community ties. However, applicants should be prepared to provide documentary evidence to substantiate any claims made in their application.

12. Rationale for Eligibility Criteria

12.1 The eligibility criteria set out in this Policy, including the requirement relating to residency, are designed to ensure that the Scheme supports applicants who have a genuine and ongoing connection to Singapore and its heritage. The Committee’s objective is not to exclude applicants who are newly arrived or who have spent time overseas, but rather to ensure that limited public funds are directed to projects that are most likely to benefit the community.

12.2 A minimum period of residency serves a practical function: it provides a clear, objective, and verifiable criterion that can be applied consistently by the Secretariat and the Committee. It also provides applicants with certainty as to whether they are eligible to apply, and reduces the scope for subjective assessment.

12.4 The eligibility criteria are therefore intended to be a threshold, not a measure of merit. Applicants who meet the threshold will be considered on the basis of the quality and feasibility of their proposed project, and on the strength of their community ties, as described in Section 11.

12.5 The Committee will keep the eligibility criteria under review, and may propose amendments to the Minister from time to time. Any such amendments will be published in accordance with Section 17.

15. Examples of Eligible Projects

15.1 The following examples are provided to illustrate the types of projects that may be supported. They are not intended to be prescriptive, and the Committee will consider each application on its own merits.

15.2 Family Histories. The Scheme may support the research and publication of a family history, including:
(a) genealogical research, including the tracing of family lines through archival records, church records, and other sources;
(b) the compilation of family trees, narratives, and supporting documents;
(c) the transcription and annotation of family documents, such as letters, diaries, and photographs;
(d) the preparation of a manuscript for publication, including editing, design, and printing.

15.3 Oral Histories. The Scheme may support the recording, transcription, and preservation of oral histories, including:
(a) interviews with individuals who have lived through significant historical events, or who have specialised knowledge of a trade, craft, or practice;
(b) the recording of interviews in any language or dialect spoken in Singapore;
(c) the transcription and translation of interviews, where appropriate;
(d) the preservation of recordings in a recognised repository, such as the National Archives of Singapore or a university library.

15.4 Community Histories. The Scheme may support projects that document the history of a particular community, such as a kampong, a religious congregation, a clan association, or a trade union. Such projects may include:
(a) the collection of photographs, documents, and other materials;
(b) the conduct of interviews with community members;
(c) the production of a publication, exhibition, or film;
(d) the creation of a website or other online resource.

The Heritage Grant Eligibility Policy 2018, eligibility_minimum_residency_years 3, required three years of residency. Record status: superseded.

15.6 Intangible Heritage. The Scheme may support projects that document or promote intangible heritage, such as:
(a) traditional crafts, including the skills and techniques of artisans;
(b) performing arts, including music, dance, and theatre;
(c) culinary traditions, including recipes, cooking techniques, and the social practices surrounding food;
(d) festivals, rituals, and other customary practices.

15.7 The Committee welcomes innovative proposals that use new technologies to document or present heritage, such as virtual reality tours, interactive maps, or crowdsourced oral history platforms. Applicants are encouraged to describe how technology will be used, and how the project will remain accessible to the public after its completion.

16. Ineligible Projects

16.1 The following types of projects are not eligible for funding under the Scheme:
(a) projects that are primarily commercial in nature, or that are undertaken for private profit;
(b) projects that are primarily academic, such as the writing of a thesis or dissertation, unless the project includes a clear public dissemination component;
(c) projects that are primarily artistic, such as the creation of a work of art, unless the work is directly related to the documentation or promotion of heritage;
(d) projects that involve the acquisition of heritage objects or collections, except where the acquisition is incidental to a larger project;
(e) projects that involve the restoration or conservation of buildings, structures, or objects, except where the restoration is incidental to a larger documentation project;
(f) projects that have already been completed, or that have already received funding from another source, unless the applicant can demonstrate that the additional funding will support a distinct and additional component of the project.

Administrative Procedures for the Review of Applications

17. Application Review Process

17.1 The review of applications under the Scheme shall proceed in the stages described in this Section. The stages are designed to ensure that each application is assessed fairly, consistently, and in accordance with the eligibility criteria set out in Sections 5 to 16 of this Policy.

17.2 The stages are as follows:

Stage 1: Receipt and Preliminary Screening
Stage 2: Technical Assessment
Stage 3: Committee Deliberation
Stage 4: Decision and Notification
Stage 5: Appeals and Reconsideration

17.3 A summary of the process is set out in the flow chart at Annex C. The flow chart is intended as a guide only; in the event of any discrepancy between the flow chart and the text of this Section, the text shall prevail.

18. Stage 1: Receipt and Preliminary Screening

18.1 Applications may be submitted electronically via the online portal, or in hard copy to the Secretariat. Hard copy applications must be received at the Secretariat’s address at 1 Canning Rise, Singapore 179868, during office hours (9.00 a.m. to 5.00 p.m., Monday to Friday, excluding public holidays).

18.2 Upon receipt, each application shall be assigned a unique application reference number. The Secretariat shall acknowledge receipt of the application by email (or by post, if no email address is provided) within five (5) working days.

18.3 The Secretariat shall conduct a preliminary screening of each application to determine whether it is complete and whether it falls within the scope of the Scheme. The preliminary screening shall include the following checks:

(a) whether the application form is duly completed and signed;
(b) whether all required supporting documents have been submitted;
(c) whether the applicant is an entity or individual that is eligible to apply under Section 5; and
(d) whether the proposed project appears to fall within the categories of eligible projects set out in Section 15, and does not appear to fall within the categories of ineligible projects set out in Section 16.

18.4 If an application is incomplete, the Secretariat shall notify the applicant in writing, specifying the missing documents or information. The applicant shall be given twenty-one (21) calendar days from the date of the notice to submit the missing documents or information. If the applicant fails to do so within the stipulated period, the application shall be considered withdrawn, unless the applicant has requested an extension of time in writing and the Secretariat has granted such extension.

18.5 If an application is complete but appears to fall outside the scope of the Scheme, the Secretariat shall refer the application to the Chair of the Policy Review Committee (the “Committee”) for a determination as to whether the application should be rejected at this stage or allowed to proceed to Stage 2. The Committee may, at its discretion, allow an application to proceed if it considers that the application raises issues of heritage significance that warrant further consideration.

18.6 The Secretariat shall record the outcome of the preliminary screening in the application file. The outcome shall be one of the following:

(a) Application complete and eligible to proceed;
(b) Application incomplete – notice issued;
(c) Application withdrawn – failure to complete; or
(d) Application rejected at preliminary screening – outside scope.

**Part VII: Stage 3 – Detailed Assessment**

19.1 Applications that pass the preliminary screening in accordance with Section 18 shall proceed to Stage 3, being the detailed assessment. The detailed assessment shall be conducted by the Secretariat, in consultation with the Committee where the Committee has directed that consultation be undertaken.

19.2 The detailed assessment shall consider the following matters:

(a) the heritage significance of the project, having regard to the criteria set out in Section 20;

(b) the feasibility of the project, including the applicant’s capacity to deliver the project within the proposed timeframe and budget;

(c) the reasonableness of the proposed budget, including whether the costs claimed are eligible costs under Section 21 and whether the applicant has obtained competitive quotations where required under Section 21.4;

(d) the applicant’s track record in managing similar projects, where applicable;

(e) the public benefit of the project, including the extent to which the project will provide opportunities for public participation, education, or engagement; and

(f) any other matter that the Committee considers relevant to the determination of the application.

19.3 The Secretariat may, at any time during the detailed assessment, request further information from the applicant in writing. The applicant shall provide the requested information within fourteen (14) calendar days from the date of the request, unless an extension of time has been granted by the Secretariat in writing.

19.4 Where the detailed assessment raises concerns about the eligibility of the project or the applicant, the Secretariat shall prepare a written assessment report and submit it to the Committee for its consideration. The report shall set out the Secretariat’s findings and recommendations, and shall be accompanied by the application file.

19.5 The Committee shall consider the assessment report and may, at its discretion:

(a) approve the application, in whole or in part;

(b) approve the application subject to conditions;

(c) defer the application for further information or clarification; or

(d) reject the application.

19.6 Where the Committee approves an application subject to conditions, the conditions shall be set out in the letter of award issued under Section 22. The applicant shall be required to comply with the conditions as a condition of receiving the Grant.

19.7 The Committee shall endeavour to complete the detailed assessment within sixty (60) calendar days from the date on which the application is deemed complete under Section 18.4. This timeline may be extended by the Committee where the complexity of the application warrants such extension.

Charter of the Singapore Family Heritage Bureau
documents.content:
ARTICLE IX: PRESERVATION AND CONSERVATION

9.1 The Bureau shall maintain a programme of preservation and conservation for all materials in its custody, having regard to the condition of the materials and the resources available to the Bureau from time to time.

9.2 The Deputy Director (Preservation) shall be responsible for the care of the collections, including:

(a) the monitoring of storage conditions, including temperature, humidity, and light levels;
(b) the inspection of materials upon accession and at such intervals as may be practicable;
(c) the repair and stabilisation of damaged materials, where feasible; and
(d) the making of surrogates, including microfilm and photographic copies, for materials of exceptional value or fragility.

9.3 Where the original of any material is at risk of deterioration, the Bureau may make a surrogate copy for research use and restrict access to the original, subject to the provisions of Article VIII.

9.4 No item in the custody of the Bureau shall be disposed of except with the approval of the Board, and any such disposal shall be recorded in the register maintained under Article X.

ARTICLE X: REGISTRATION AND CATALOGUING

10.1 The Registrar shall maintain a register of all materials accessioned by the Bureau, showing in respect of each item:

(a) the date of accession;
(b) the name and address of the donor;
(c) a description of the material;
(d) any conditions attached to its use; and
(e) the present location of the material.

10.2 The Bureau shall prepare catalogues and finding aids to the collections and shall update them from time to time as may be practicable.

10.3 The Registrar shall assign a unique accession number to each item or group of items, and such number shall be marked on the material or its container in a manner that does not damage the material.

ARTICLE XI: PUBLIC SERVICES AND OUTREACH

11.1 The Head of Public Services shall be responsible for the reading room and for assisting members of the public in their use of the collections.

11.2 The reading room shall be open on such days and at such hours as the Board may determine, and the rules for its use shall be posted therein.

11.3 The Bureau shall, through its Head of Outreach, organise programmes to encourage public interest in family history and in the preservation of family records. Such programmes may include exhibitions, talks, workshops, and publications.

11.4 The Bureau may cooperate with schools, universities, and other institutions in Singapore and abroad for the purpose of advancing genealogical research and the preservation of family heritage.

ARTICLE XII: PUBLICATIONS

12.1 The Bureau may publish such catalogues, guides, and other works as may further its objects.

12.2 All publications of the Bureau shall acknowledge the sources from which the materials reproduced therein are drawn, and shall comply with any conditions attached to the use of such materials.

ARTICLE XIII: FINANCE

13.1 The funds of the Bureau shall consist of:

(a) grants and subventions from the Government of Singapore;
(b) donations and bequests;
(c) fees for services rendered; and
(d) such other moneys as may lawfully be received by the Bureau.

13.2 The accounts of the Bureau shall be kept in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles and shall be audited annually by an auditor appointed by the Board.

13.3 No member of the Board or officer of the Bureau shall benefit personally from any transaction entered into on behalf of the Bureau, except for the reimbursement of expenses properly incurred.

documents.content:
Research Grants are intended to support original genealogical research that contributes to the public understanding of Singapore's social history. These grants may be used to defray the costs of travel to archives, purchase of reproductions of records, engagement of research assistants, and transcription services.

4.2 Publication Grants

Publication Grants are intended to support the production and dissemination of genealogical works, including printed family histories, digital databases, and curated exhibitions. Publication Grants may cover printing costs, editorial services, and the development of accompanying educational materials.

4.3 Community Engagement Grants

Community Engagement Grants are intended for Family Associations and Voluntary Welfare Organisations that wish to organise workshops, talks, or outreach programmes to encourage broader participation in genealogical research within their communities.

4.4 The maximum amount that may be awarded under any single Grant is subject to the limits specified in the Scheme's Funding Guidelines, which are issued separately and updated from time to time. Applicants are encouraged to consult the latest edition of the Funding Guidelines before submitting an application.

5. APPLICATION PROCEDURE (SUMMARY)

5.1 Applications must be submitted on the prescribed form, available from the Scheme's website or from the National Heritage Board's Resource Centre.

5.2 Each application must include a detailed project proposal, a budget breakdown, and a timeline for completion. Supporting documents, such as letters of endorsement from community organisations or evidence of prior research, may be attached.

5.3 Applications are assessed in the order in which they are received. The Committee aims to inform applicants of its decision within eight (8) weeks of receipt of a complete application.

5.4 Transitional Arrangements: Applicants who submitted a complete application before 01 July 2018 but have not yet received a decision will have their application assessed under the provisions of the previous Policy (Version 1.0), except where the current Policy is more favourable to the applicant.

6. REVIEW AND APPROVAL PROCESS

6.1 All applications are reviewed by at least two members of the Committee, who will assess the application against the eligibility criteria set out in the separate Eligibility Criteria Schedule (Annex A).

6.2 The Committee may, at its discretion, seek external expert opinion on the technical merits of a proposed project.

6.3 The Committee's decision is final. No correspondence will be entertained regarding the merits of individual applications.

7. ENQUIRIES

Enquiries regarding this Policy may be directed to:

Policy Review Committee
National Heritage Board
61 Stamford Road
Singapore 178892

Email: hgs_policy@nhb.gov.sg

**HERITAGE GRANT ELIGIBILITY POLICY (VERSION 2.0, 2018)**

**8. DURATION AND TRANSITION ARRANGEMENTS**

8.1 This Policy shall take effect on 01 July 2018 and shall remain in force until 30 June 2020, unless extended or earlier revised by the Policy Review Committee. The Committee will undertake a formal review of the Policy no later than the first quarter of 2020, with a view to determining whether the Scheme should be continued, amended, or allowed to lapse.

8.2 The Heritage Grant Scheme, effective_end_date 2020-06-30, concluded its initial phase. Record status: superseded. Applications received after that date will not be considered under this Policy, and applicants are advised to refer to any subsequent policy document that may be issued in its place.

8.3 Where an applicant has been informed in writing that their application has been approved but the grant agreement has not yet been executed as at the effective_end_date, the Committee may, at its absolute discretion, proceed with the execution of the agreement, subject to the availability of funds.

8.4 Any grant awarded under this Policy remains subject to the terms and conditions set out in the Grant Agreement, including the requirement to submit progress reports and a final report within the timeframes specified therein.

**9. APPLICATION PROCEDURES**

9.1 Applications shall be made on the prescribed application form, which may be obtained from the National Heritage Board website or requested by post, email, or in person at the address given in Section 7.

9.2 The application form shall be completed in full and accompanied by the following supporting documents:

(a) A detailed project proposal, including the project title, objectives, methodology, expected outcomes, and a timeline for completion;

(b) A detailed budget, indicating the total project cost, the amount of grant requested, and the sources of any other funding, whether confirmed or pending;

(c) A curriculum vitae of the principal applicant and, where applicable, of any co-applicants or key personnel;

(d) Where the applicant is an organisation, a copy of its constitution or memorandum and articles of association, and its latest annual report or financial statements, if available;

(e) Letters of support from at least two referees who are able to comment on the applicant’s capability to undertake the proposed project; and

(f) Any other documents that the Committee may reasonably require to assess the application.

9.3 Incomplete applications will be returned to the applicant for resubmission. The date of receipt of a complete application shall be recorded by the Secretariat and shall be used for the purposes of Section 5.3.

9.4 The Secretariat shall acknowledge receipt of each complete application within five (5) working days. The acknowledgement shall include the application reference number, which the applicant should quote in all subsequent correspondence.

9.5 Applications may be submitted at any time during the period of this Policy. There is no fixed application window, and the Committee will consider applications on a rolling basis, subject to the availability of funds.

9.6 The Committee reserves the right to close the Scheme to new applications at any time if the allocated budget for the financial year has been fully committed. Notice of such closure shall be published on the National Heritage Board website and, where practicable, communicated to applicants who have not yet submitted an application.

10.2 The principles in Section 10.1 are intended to guide the Committee’s exercise of discretion under this Policy. They are not exhaustive, and the Committee may take into account any other factors it considers relevant in the circumstances of a particular application. Conversely, the fact that a project satisfies one or more of these principles does not guarantee that it will be considered eligible.

11. Community Ties

11.1 The Committee recognises that heritage is rooted in communities, and that projects are most likely to be effective when they are grounded in strong community ties. Accordingly, applicants are encouraged to demonstrate, in their project proposal, the nature and extent of their connections to the community or communities that are the subject of the project.

11.2 Community ties may be demonstrated in a variety of ways, including but not limited to:

(a) A record of prior involvement with the community, whether in a personal, professional, or volunteer capacity;

(b) Letters of support from community leaders, religious institutions, clan associations, or other local bodies;

(c) Evidence of past projects or activities undertaken with or for the community;

(d) A description of the applicant’s current relationship with the community, including any ongoing commitments or responsibilities; and

(e) Any other evidence that the applicant considers relevant to demonstrating community ties.

11.4 The Committee will consider the totality of the evidence provided, and will not apply a fixed formula in assessing community ties. However, applicants should be prepared to provide documentary evidence to substantiate any claims made in their application.

Sticky note (attached to Section 11.4, handwritten in green ink): “Agree with H.L. We should state a number of years. Otherwise officers will have no guidance. — A.S.”

12. Rationale for Eligibility Criteria

12.1 The eligibility criteria set out in this Policy, including the requirement relating to residency, are designed to ensure that the Scheme supports applicants who have a genuine and ongoing connection to Singapore and its heritage. The Committee’s objective is not to exclude applicants who are newly arrived or who have spent time overseas, but rather to ensure that limited public funds are directed to projects that are most likely to benefit the community.

12.2 A minimum period of residency serves a practical function: it provides a clear, objective, and verifiable criterion that can be applied consistently by the Secretariat and the Committee. It also provides applicants with certainty as to whether they are eligible to apply, and reduces the scope for subjective assessment.

12.4 The eligibility criteria are therefore intended to be a threshold, not a measure of merit. Applicants who meet the threshold will be considered on the basis of the quality and feasibility of their proposed project, and on the strength of their community ties, as described in Section 11.

12.5 The Committee will keep the eligibility criteria under review, and may propose amendments to the Minister from time to time. Any such amendments will be published in accordance with Section 17.

Sticky note (attached to Section 12.2, handwritten in blue ink): “Good. But we need to be careful that the number we choose is defensible. 5 years is common in other schemes. — A.S.”

13.1 The Heritage Grant Eligibility Policy 2020, eligibility_minimum_residency_years 5, requires five years of residency. Record status: current. This requirement applies to the principal applicant, and to any co-applicant who is an individual.

Administrative Procedures for the Review of Applications

17. Application Review Process

17.1 The review of applications under the Scheme shall proceed in the stages described in this Section. The stages are designed to ensure that each application is assessed fairly, consistently, and in accordance with the eligibility criteria set out in Sections 5 to 16 of this Policy.

17.2 The stages are as follows:

Stage 1: Receipt and Preliminary Screening
Stage 2: Technical Assessment
Stage 3: Committee Deliberation
Stage 4: Decision and Notification
Stage 5: Appeals and Reconsideration

17.3 A summary of the process is set out in the flow chart at Annex C. The flow chart is intended as a guide only; in the event of any discrepancy between the flow chart and the text of this Section, the text shall prevail.

18. Stage 1: Receipt and Preliminary Screening

18.1 Applications may be submitted electronically via the online portal, or in hard copy to the Secretariat. Hard copy applications must be received at the Secretariat’s address at 1 Canning Rise, Singapore 179868, during office hours (9.00 a.m. to 5.00 p.m., Monday to Friday, excluding public holidays).

18.2 Upon receipt, each application shall be assigned a unique application reference number. The Secretariat shall acknowledge receipt of the application by email (or by post, if no email address is provided) within five (5) working days.

18.3 The Secretariat shall conduct a preliminary screening of each application to determine whether it is complete and whether it falls within the scope of the Scheme. The preliminary screening shall include the following checks:

(a) whether the application form is duly completed and signed;
(b) whether all required supporting documents have been submitted;
(c) whether the applicant is an entity or individual that is eligible to apply under Section 5; and
(d) whether the proposed project appears to fall within the categories of eligible projects set out in Section 15, and does not appear to fall within the categories of ineligible projects set out in Section 16.

18.4 If an application is incomplete, the Secretariat shall notify the applicant in writing, specifying the missing documents or information. The applicant shall be given twenty-one (21) calendar days from the date of the notice to submit the missing documents or information. If the applicant fails to do so within the stipulated period, the application shall be considered withdrawn, unless the applicant has requested an extension of time in writing and the Secretariat has granted such extension.

18.5 If an application is complete but appears to fall outside the scope of the Scheme, the Secretariat shall refer the application to the Chair of the Policy Review Committee (the “Committee”) for a determination as to whether the application should be rejected at this stage or allowed to proceed to Stage 2. The Committee may, at its discretion, allow an application to proceed if it considers that the application raises issues of heritage significance that warrant further consideration.

18.6 The Secretariat shall record the outcome of the preliminary screening in the application file. The outcome shall be one of the following:

(a) Application complete and eligible to proceed;
(b) Application incomplete – notice issued;
(c) Application withdrawn – failure to complete; or
(d) Application rejected at preliminary screening – outside scope.

POLICY REGISTRY OF THE HERITAGE GRANT SCHEME
Maintained by the Archives and Records Unit, Singapore Family Heritage Board (SFHB)

Purpose
This registry records the version history, effective dates, and current status of all policy documents relating to the Heritage Grant Scheme. It serves as the authoritative reference for determining which version of a policy was in force at any given time. Staff should consult this registry before processing applications or responding to queries about eligibility.

Note on Archival Integrity
Entries in this registry are made at the time of approval and are not altered retrospectively. Where a policy has been revised, the superseded version remains listed for historical reference, and the current version is indicated accordingly. Any correction to an entry requires the approval of the Archives and Records Unit and must be accompanied by a cross-reference to the authorising memo.

Heritage Grant Eligibility Policy 2020

This registry is updated within five working days of any policy approval. Please direct any discrepancies or missing entries to the Archives and Records Unit.
